content: The treatment regimens for tuberculosis (TB) described in the text are highly specific and tailored to the severity of the disease, patient age, and drug resistance profiles. Below is a detailed explanation of the regimens and their clinical considerations: 1. Shorter Regimens for Less Severe TB: For children aged 12 years or older (weighing ≥30 kg), bedaquiline was administered for at least 6 months. This could be extended to 9 months if there was delayed smear or culture conversion, or if second-line drug susceptibility test results were unavailable or uninterpretable. The intensive phase lasted 4 months but could be extended to 6 months based on treatment response (e.g., smear conversion and clinical improvement at month 4). The continuation phase lasted 5 months, resulting in a total treatment duration of 9–11 months for most patients. For children aged 6–12 years (weighing 15–30 kg), the injectable drug was replaced with delamanid. The regimen included 4–6 months of linezolid (2 months), delamanid (6 months), levofloxacin, clofazimine, high-dose isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, followed by 5 months of levofloxacin, clofazimine, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. For children under 6 years (weighing <15 kg), the regimen included 4–6 months of linezolid (2 months), para-aminosalicylic acid, levofloxacin, clofazimine, high-dose isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, followed by 5 months of levofloxacin, clofazimine, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. 2. Longer Regimens (≥18 Months): The standard longer regimen consisted of at least 18 months of bedaquiline, levofloxacin, linezolid, terizidone, and clofazimine. Modifications were allowed based on specific clinical scenarios: Patients with rifampicin-resistant TB meningitis received a longer individualized regimen including delamanid, pyrazinamide, and high-dose isoniazid or ethionamide. Patients with resistance to bedaquiline, linezolid, or clofazimine were treated with individualized regimens based on expert committee advice. Patients with hemoglobin levels below 8 g/dL did not receive linezolid; instead, two additional WHO Group C drugs, including delamanid, were used. Patients with persistent culture positivity after 9–12 months of treatment could transition to the longer regimen. 3. Analytic Issues in Cohort Studies: The South African 2019 cohort was divided into short-course and longer-course treatment groups based on clinical and microbiological characteristics. This introduced potential confounding by indication, making direct comparisons of regimen effectiveness within the dataset challenging. Comparisons with the South African 9–12 month regimen must account for the less severe disease in this cohort. Differences in treatment duration (9–12 months vs. ≥18 months) also mean that patients in the shorter regimen group interact with the TB program for a shorter time, potentially reducing the reporting of non-TB-related deaths or serious adverse events unrelated to the regimen. This could introduce bias when comparing outcomes between groups. 4. WHO Individual Patient Data (IPD) 2021 Dataset: This dataset includes 14 cohorts of patients treated with standardized oral regimens (18–24 months) containing bedaquiline, with some also including linezolid. These cohorts serve as a comparator group for evaluating shorter regimens (6–9 months). The dataset highlights the importance of follow-up time in assessing relapse rates, particularly for shorter regimens. Follow-up time is measured from the start of treatment to minimize the effect of differences in total follow-up time. 5. NEXT Trial: This Phase II/III trial in South Africa evaluated a 6–9 month all-oral regimen (linezolid, bedaquiline, levofloxacin, terizidone, pyrazinamide, and ethionamide or high-dose isoniazid) for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). Treatment was individualized based on genotypic testing, and therapy was stopped after three consecutive negative cultures. The comparator was the local standard of care, which included longer regimens (18–20 months or 9–12 months) with injectable antibiotics. 6. NIX-TB Study: This Phase III study assessed the safety and efficacy of a 6-month regimen of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (1200 mg daily) for extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) or treatment-intolerant/non-responsive MDR-TB. Treatment could be extended to 9 months for patients who remained culture-positive at month 4. The primary outcome was the incidence of bacteriologic or clinical failure or relapse within 6 months after treatment completion. 7. ZENIX Study: This Phase III trial evaluated the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of varying doses and durations of linezolid in combination with bedaquiline and pretomanid for pulmonary XDR-TB, pre-XDR-TB, or treatment-intolerant/non-responsive MDR-TB. Participants were randomized into four groups with different linezolid regimens (1200 mg for 26 weeks, 1200 mg for 9 weeks, 600 mg for 26 weeks, and 600 mg for 9 weeks). The study was conducted in Russia, Moldova, and South Africa. 8. Challenges in Comparing Regimens: Differences in follow-up times between cohorts complicate comparisons of outcomes. For shorter regimens, post-treatment follow-up is critical to capture relapse rates. When comparing shorter and longer regimens, it may be necessary to truncate the follow-up period for longer regimens to ensure equivalent total follow-up time, which could slightly underestimate relapse rates in the longer regimen cohort. These findings underscore the complexity of treating drug-resistant TB and the need for individualized regimens based on patient characteristics, drug resistance profiles, and clinical response.
